`sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds`\n\nSet `sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds` on servers so inactive sessions are cleaned up automatically. This prevents zombie sessions in long-running processes and reduces memory and filesystem pressure.\n\n| Language | Public option |\n|----------|---------------|\n| TypeScript | `sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds` |\n| Python | `session_idle_timeout_seconds` |\n| Go | `SessionIdleTimeoutSeconds` |\n| .NET | `SessionIdleTimeoutSeconds` |\n| Java | `setSessionIdleTimeoutSeconds(...)` |\n| Rust | `with_session_idle_timeout_seconds(...)` |\n\nUse a value that matches your product's conversation lifetime. For chat backends, 15 to 30 minutes is usually a good starting point. For workflow agents, use a longer timeout and explicit deletion when the workflow completes.\n\n### `baseDirectory`\n\n`baseDirectory` sets `COPILOT_HOME` for a runtime instance. Use it to isolate runtime state, credentials, and session data per process, pod, worker, or tenant boundary.\n\n```typescript\nimport { CopilotClient } from \"@github/copilot-sdk\";\n\nconst client = new CopilotClient({\n    mode: \"empty\",\n    baseDirectory: `/var/lib/my-app/copilot/runtime-${process.env.HOSTNAME}`,\n    sessionIdleTimeoutSeconds: 900,\n});\n```\n\nThe runtime stores session state under the configured `COPILOT_HOME`, including `session-state/{sessionId}`. If your app runs multiple runtime instances, give each instance a distinct directory unless you intentionally use shared storage.\n\nWhen the SDK connects to an already-running runtime with `RuntimeConnection.forUri(url)`, `baseDirectory` is ignored by the SDK client. Configure `COPILOT_HOME` on the runtime process instead.\n\n### `sessionFs`\n\n`sessionFs` registers a custom session filesystem provider so session-scoped file I/O can be routed through application storage instead of the runtime's local disk. Use it when local disk is ephemeral, when session state needs to live in object storage, or when a platform needs to enforce tenant-aware storage paths.\n\n```typescript\nimport { CopilotClient } from \"@github/copilot-sdk\";\n\nconst client = new CopilotClient({\n    mode: \"empty\",\n    sessionFs: {\n        initialCwd: \"/workspace\",\n        sessionStatePath: \"/session-state\",\n        conventions: \"posix\",\n    },\n});\n```\n\nFor languages that expose a provider callback, configure `sessionFs` at the client level and provide a per-session filesystem handler when creating or resuming a session. See [Session Persistence](../features/session-persistence.md) for persistence concepts and storage trade-offs.\n\nRuntime-owned durable permission choices also use the session filesystem. Under the provider's `sessionStatePath`, `permissions.json` retains its top-level `locations` map with `tool_approvals` and `allowed_directories`; `settings.json` stores top-level `allowedUrls` and `sandbox`; and `config.json` stores top-level `trustedFolders`.\n\nURL approvals are read only from `settings.json`; legacy user-setting fields such as `allowedUrls` in `config.json` are ignored, matching host behavior.\n\nLocation keys are normalized provider directory paths, with no added prefix. Resolution follows the provider's path conventions without inspecting the host filesystem or discovering host Git repositories. `/workspace` and `/workspace/sub` select different location entries.\n\nThe runtime does not add session-ID partitions to these files or change their sharing granularity. Sessions accessing the same files in the same provider namespace share remembered grants. Your application must use distinct namespaces for tenants or sessions that require isolation, authorize access to each namespace, and reconnect resumed sessions to their original namespace.\n\nWith a separate namespace per session, permanent grants survive that session's resumes rather than becoming tenant-wide grants for new sessions. Sharing grants across sessions requires sharing the consent files while keeping other session state separate. The runtime serializes consent updates only within the same provider endpoint and process; applications that share backing files across endpoints or processes must coordinate concurrent updates.\n\nThe runtime blocks direct provider-backed file writes to the lexical approval-metadata paths as defense in depth, not as a tamper-proof storage boundary. Providers must not expose writable aliases (such as symlinks or Windows 8.3 short names) to approval metadata through agent file tools. Shell tools do not run through SessionFS, and their commands are not checked against its virtual metadata paths. If your application separately exposes the provider's backing storage to shell execution or other arbitrary code, your host must protect that storage.\n\nSession filesystem approval operations never import or fall back to remembered permissions from the host's `permissions-config.json`, URL or sandbox settings from `settings.json`, or folder trust from `config.json`. They do not update those host files, even when the provider has no approvals or reports an error. A provider error is not permission to use host consent. URL deny rules remain authoritative, and folder trust uses provider paths without host Git discovery.\n\nApprove-once, approve-for-session, rejections, and session policy changes retain their existing lifetimes and event-replay behavior. Storage routing does not turn them into new permanent grants. Protect session transcripts, including durable permission events, with the same tenant isolation as approval metadata.\n\nThis boundary applies only to sessions using a session filesystem provider. All SDK applications without `sessionFs`, in both `empty` and `copilot-cli` modes, and ordinary CLI sessions retain existing host-backed persistence for remembered locations, permanent URL approvals, folder trust, and sandbox settings.\n\nVerified public SDK surfaces:\n\n| Language | Client-level config | Per-session provider |\n|----------|---------------------|----------------------|\n| TypeScript | `sessionFs` | `createSessionFsProvider` |\n| Python | `session_fs` | `create_session_fs_handler` |\n| Go | `SessionFS` | `CreateSessionFSProvider` |\n| .NET | `SessionFs` | `CreateSessionFsProvider` |\n| Rust | `with_session_fs(...)` | `with_session_fs_provider(...)` |\n\nJava does not currently expose a verified public `sessionFs` option, so this guide does not show a Java `sessionFs` sample.\n\n### `RuntimeConnection.forUri(url)`\n\nUse an external runtime connection when multiple SDK clients should share one already-running runtime. Here is the raw content:\nContents of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/copilot-sdk/d1e6021a43b26e87acfcd43b37988eff09dd8aaf/docs/features/agent-loop.md:\n# The agent loop\n\nHow the Copilot CLI processes a user message end-to-end: from prompt to `session.idle`.\n\n## Architecture\n\n```mermaid\ngraph LR\n    App[\"Your App\"] -->|send prompt| SDK[\"SDK Session\"]\n    SDK -->|JSON-RPC| CLI[\"Copilot CLI\"]\n    CLI -->|API calls| LLM[\"LLM\"]\n    LLM -->|response| CLI\n    CLI -->|events| SDK\n    SDK -->|events| App\n```\n\nThe **SDK** is a transport layer—it sends your prompt to the **Copilot CLI** over JSON-RPC and surfaces events back to your app. The **CLI** is the orchestrator that runs the agentic tool-use loop, making one or more LLM API calls until the task is done.\n\n## The tool-use loop\n\nWhen you call `session.send({ prompt })`, the CLI enters a loop:\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TD\n    A[\"User prompt\"] --> B[\"LLM API call\\n(= one turn)\"]\n    B --> C{\"toolRequests\\nin response?\"}\n    C -->|Yes| D[\"Execute tools\\nCollect results\"]\n    D -->|\"Results fed back\\nas next turn input\"| B\n    C -->|No| E[\"Final text\\nresponse\"]\n    E --> F([\"session.idle\"])\n\n    style B fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#58a6ff,color:#c9d1d9\n    style D fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#3fb950,color:#c9d1d9\n    style F fill:#0d1117,stroke:#f0883e,color:#f0883e\n```\n\nThe model sees the **full conversation history** on each call—system prompt, user message, and all prior tool calls and results.\n\n**Key insight:** Each iteration of this loop is exactly one LLM API call, visible as one `assistant.turn_start` / `assistant.turn_end` pair in the event log. There are no hidden calls.\n\n## Multiple tool calls\n\nSession creation and resume accept `allowMultipleToolCalls` in TypeScript and Java,\n`AllowMultipleToolCalls` in Go and .NET, and `allow_multiple_tool_calls` in Python\nand Rust. Omitted or `true` preserves the default: the model can request multiple\ntools in one response and the runtime can execute their handlers concurrently.\n\nSet it to `false` to ask the provider for at most one tool call per response.\nThe runtime sends OpenAI's `parallel_tool_calls: false` or Anthropic's\n`disable_parallel_tool_use: true`. This is a provider hint, not an execution\nguarantee; some compatible providers do not support it. If the provider returns\nmultiple calls anyway, the runtime handles all of them using its existing\nexecution policy. It does not discard calls, serialize handlers, or rewrite\nsystem instructions. Applications that require serialized access to a resource\nmust coordinate that access in their handlers.\n\nSubagents inherit the preference. Omission on a resident resume preserves the\ncurrent value; after a cold resume, supply it again. Changing it on resume can\ninvalidate the provider's prompt cache. There is no separate runtime execution\nmode or live-update option.\n\n## Turns—what they are\n\nA **turn** is a single LLM API call and its consequences:\n\n1. The CLI sends the conversation history to the LLM\n1. The LLM responds (possibly with tool requests)\n1. If tools were requested, the CLI executes them\n1. `assistant.turn_end` is emitted\n\nA single user message typically results in **multiple turns**. For example, a question like \"how does X work in this codebase?\" might produce:\n\n| Turn | What the model does | toolRequests? |\n|------|-------------------|---------------|\n| 1 | Calls `grep` and `glob` to search the codebase | ✅ Yes |\n| 2 | Reads specific files based on search results | ✅ Yes |\n| 3 | Reads more files for deeper context | ✅ Yes |\n| 4 | Produces the final text answer | ❌ No → loop ends |\n\nThe model decides on each turn whether to request more tools or produce a final answer. Each call sees the **full accumulated context** (all prior tool calls and results), so it can make an informed decision about whether it has enough information.\n\n## Event flow for a multi-turn interaction\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TD\n    send[\"session.send({ prompt: &quot;Fix the bug in auth.ts&quot; })\"]\n\n    subgraph Turn1 [\"Turn 1\"]\n        t1s[\"assistant.turn_start\"]\n        t1m[\"assistant.message (toolRequests)\"]\n        t1ts[\"tool.execution_start (read_file)\"]\n        t1tc[\"tool.execution_complete\"]\n        t1e[\"assistant.turn_end\"]\n        t1s --> t1m --> t1ts --> t1tc --> t1e\n    end\n\n    subgraph Turn2 [\"Turn 2 — auto-triggered by CLI\"]\n        t2s[\"assistant.turn_start\"]\n        t2m[\"assistant.message (toolRequests)\"]\n        t2ts[\"tool.execution_start (edit_file)\"]\n        t2tc[\"tool.execution_complete\"]\n        t2e[\"assistant.turn_end\"]\n        t2s --> t2m --> t2ts --> t2tc --> t2e\n    end\n\n    subgraph Turn3 [\"Turn 3\"]\n        t3s[\"assistant.turn_start\"]\n        t3m[\"assistant.message (no toolRequests)\\n&quot;Done, here's what I changed&quot;\"]\n        t3e[\"assistant.turn_end\"]\n        t3s --> t3m --> t3e\n    end\n\n    idle([\"session.idle — ready for next message\"])\n\n    send --> Turn1 --> Turn2 --> Turn3 --> idle\n```\n\n## Who triggers each turn?\n\n| Actor | Responsibility |\n|-------|---------------|\n| **Your app** | Sends the initial prompt via `session.send()` |\n| **Copilot CLI** | Runs the tool-use loop—executes tools and feeds results back to the LLM for the next turn |\n| **LLM** | Decides whether to request tools (continue looping) or produce a final response (stop) |\n| **SDK** | Passes events through; does not control the loop |\n\nThe CLI is purely mechanical: \"model asked for tools → execute → call model again.\" The **model** is the decision-maker for when to stop.\n\n## `session.idle` vs `session.task_complete`\n\nThese are two different completion signals with very different guarantees:\n\n### `session.idle`\n\n* **Always emitted** when the tool-use loop ends\n* **Ephemeral**: not persisted to disk, not replayed on session resume\n* Means: \"the agent has stopped processing and is ready for the next message\"\n* **Use this** as your reliable \"done\" signal\n\nThe SDK's `sendAndWait()` method waits for this event:\n\n```typescript\n// Blocks until session.idle fires\nconst response = await session.sendAndWait({ prompt: \"Fix the bug\" });\n```\n\n### `session.task_complete`\n\n* **Optionally emitted**: requires the model to explicitly signal it\n* **Persisted**: saved to the session event log on disk\n* Means: \"the agent considers the overall task fulfilled\"\n* Carries an optional `summary` field\n\n```typescript\nsession.on(\"session.task_complete\", (event) => {\n    console.log(\"Task done:\", event.data.summary);\n});\n```\n\n### Autopilot mode: the CLI nudges for `task_complete`\n\nIn **autopilot mode** (headless/autonomous operation), the CLI actively tracks whether the model has called `task_complete`. If the tool-use loop ends without it, the CLI injects a synthetic user message nudging the model:\n\n> *\"You have not yet marked the task as complete using the task_complete tool. If you were planning changes the user asked for, stop planning and start implementing. You aren't done until you have fully completed the task.\"*\n\nThis effectively restarts the tool-use loop—the model sees the nudge as a new user message and continues working. The nudge also instructs the model **not** to call `task_complete` prematurely:\n\n* Don't call it if you have open questions—make decisions and keep working\n* Don't call it if you hit an error—try to resolve it\n* Don't call it if there are remaining steps—complete them first\n\nThe one exception is a request that only asked for a review, analysis or recommendation: once that has been delivered, the nudge tells the model to call `task_complete` rather than start a follow-up it offered.\n\nThis creates a **two-level completion mechanism** in autopilot:\n1. The model calls `task_complete` with a summary → CLI emits `session.task_complete` → done\n1. The model stops without calling it → CLI nudges → model continues or calls `task_complete`\n\nCompleting or pausing an autopilot objective leaves the session in autopilot mode by default, matching the interactive CLI. The objective still completes or pauses, and the run can become idle; keeping the mode selected does not keep working on a finished objective. To opt into automatic restoration to interactive mode, call `session.rpc.autopilotObjective.setStayInAutopilot({ value: false })`. To switch mode immediately, call `session.rpc.mode.set({ mode: \"interactive\" })`.\n\n### Why `task_complete` might not appear\n\nIn **interactive mode** (normal chat), the CLI does not nudge for `task_complete`. The model may skip it entirely. Common reasons:\n\n* **Conversational Q&A**: The model answers a question and simply stops—there's no discrete \"task\" to complete\n* **Model discretion**: The model produces a final text response without calling the task-complete signal\n* **Interrupted sessions**: The session ends before the model reaches a completion point\n\nThe CLI emits `session.idle` regardless, because it's a mechanical signal (the loop ended), not a semantic one (the model thinks it's done).\n\n### Which should you use?\n\n| Use case | Signal |\n|----------|--------|\n| \"Wait for the agent to finish processing\" | `session.idle` ✅ |\n| \"Know when a coding task is done\" | `session.task_complete` (best-effort) |\n| \"Timeout/error handling\" | `session.idle` + `session.error` ✅ |\n\n## Counting LLM calls\n\nThe number of `assistant.turn_start` / `assistant.turn_end` pairs in the event log equals the total number of LLM API calls made. There are no hidden calls for planning, evaluation, or completion checking.\n\nTo inspect turn count for a session:\n\n```typescript\nconst turns = (await session.getEvents()).filter((event) => event.type === \"assistant.turn_start\").length;\n```\n\n## Further reading\n\n* [Streaming Events Reference](./streaming-events.md): Field-level reference for the event types applications most often handle\n* [Session Persistence](./session-persistence.md): How sessions are saved and resumed\n* [Hooks](./hooks.md): Intercepting events in the loop (permissions, tools)\n"

You can use it to answer questions, write and debug code, and interact with GitHub.com. For example, you can ask Copilot to make some changes to a project and create a pull request.\n\nGitHub Copilot CLI gives you quick access to a powerful AI agent, without having to leave your terminal. It can help you complete tasks more quickly by working on your behalf, and you can work iteratively with GitHub Copilot CLI to build the code you need.\n\n## Supported operating systems\n\n* Linux\n* macOS\n* Windows from within Powershell and [Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/about)\n\nFor installation instructions, see [Installing GitHub Copilot CLI](/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/set-up-copilot-cli/install-copilot-cli).\n\n## Modes of use\n\nGitHub Copilot CLI has two user interfaces: interactive and programmatic.\n\n### Interactive interface\n\nTo start an interactive session, enter `copilot`. Within an interactive session, you can have a conversation with Copilot. You can prompt Copilot to perform one or more tasks, and you can give it feedback and steer the direction of the work.\n\n![Screenshot of the Welcome message in the interactive interface of Copilot.](/assets/images/help/copilot/copilot-cli-welcome.png)\n\nThe interactive interface has two modes. In addition to the default ask/execute mode there is also a **plan mode** in which Copilot will build a structured implementation plan for a task you want to complete.\n\nPress <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Tab</kbd> to cycle between modes. In plan mode, Copilot analyzes your request, asks clarifying questions to understand scope and requirements, and builds a plan before writing any code. This helps you catch misunderstandings before any code is written, and stay in control of complex, multi-step tasks.\n\n### Programmatic interface\n\nYou can also pass the CLI a single prompt directly on the command line. The CLI completes the task and then exits.\n\nTo use the CLI programmatically, include the `-p` or `--prompt` command-line option in your command. To allow Copilot to modify and execute files you should also use one of the approval options described later in this article—see [Allowing tools to be used without manual approval](#allowing-tools-to-be-used-without-manual-approval) ). For example:\n\n```bash copy\ncopilot -p \"Show me this week's commits and summarize them\" --allow-tool='shell(git)'\n```\n\nAlternatively, you can use a script to output command-line options and pipe this to `copilot`. For example:\n\n```bash copy\n./script-outputting-options.sh | copilot\n```\n\n> [!CAUTION]\n> If you use an automatic approval option such as `--allow-all-tools`, Copilot has the same access as you do to files on your computer, and can run any shell commands that you can run, without getting your prior approval. See [Security considerations](#security-considerations), later in this article.\n\n## Running Copilot CLI commands in a sandbox\n\nTo prevent Copilot from modifying files you don't want it to touch, you can force agents to run commands within a local sandboxed environment. Alternatively, you can run an entire CLI session in an isolated environment in the cloud. For more information, see [About local sandboxing for GitHub Copilot](/en/copilot/concepts/about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes).\n\n### Local sandboxing\n\nYou can enable local sandboxing inside a Copilot CLI session to restrict Copilot's access to your filesystem, network, and system capabilities. To enable it, run `/sandbox enable` inside a session.\n\n### Cloud sandboxing\n\nYou can start a Copilot CLI session in a cloud sandbox. The `--cloud` option starts the same kind of cloud sandbox as other Copilot clients, so the session runs in an isolated environment that GitHub hosts, without using your machine.\n\nBecause the session runs in the cloud, you can follow and steer it from any Copilot client. For example, you can start work in Copilot CLI, steer it from GitHub Mobile while away, then pick it back up in Copilot CLI or another client. For more information, see [About cloud sandboxes for GitHub Copilot](/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/about-cloud-sandboxes).\n\nTo start a cloud-backed session, run:\n\n```bash copy\ncopilot --cloud\n```\n\n## Use cases for GitHub Copilot CLI\n\nThe following sections provide examples of tasks you can complete with GitHub Copilot CLI.\n\n### Local tasks\n\n* From within a project directory you can ask Copilot to make a change to the code in the project. For example:\n\n  `Change the background-color of H1 headings to dark blue`\n\n  Copilot finds the CSS file where H1 headings are defined and changes the color value.\n\n* Ask Copilot to tell you about changes to a file:\n\n  `Show me the last 5 changes made to the CHANGELOG.md file. Who changed the file, when, and give a brief summary of the changes they made`\n\n* Use Copilot to help you improve the code, or documentation, in your project.\n\n  * `Suggest improvements to content.js`\n\n  * `Rewrite the readme in this project to make it more accessible to newcomers`\n\n* Use Copilot to help you perform Git operations.\n\n  * `Commit the changes to this repo`\n\n  * `Revert the last commit, leaving the changes unstaged`\n\n* Ask Copilot to create an application from scratch—for example, as a proof of concept.\n\n  `Use the create-next-app kit and tailwind CSS to create a next.js app. The app should be a dashboard built with data from the GitHub API. It should track this project's build success rate, average build duration, number of failed builds, and automated test pass rate. After creating the app, give me easy to follow instructions on how to build, run, and view the app in my browser.`\n\n* Ask Copilot to explain why a change it made is not working as expected, or tell Copilot to fix a problem with the last change it made. For example:\n\n  `You said: \"The application is now running on http://localhost:3002 and is fully functional!\" but when I browse to that URL I get \"This site can't be reached\"`\n\n### Computer use\n\nIn local sessions on macOS and Windows, you can enable computer use to let Copilot interact with desktop applications. This capability is useful for workflows in legacy and GUI-only software that do not provide an API, command-line interface, or MCP integration. For more information, see [About computer use in GitHub Copilot](/en/copilot/concepts/agent-capabilities/agent-powered-workflows-and-operations/computer-use).\n\n### Tasks involving GitHub.com\n\n* Fetch and display details about your work from GitHub.com.\n\n  * `List my open PRs`\n\n    This lists your open pull requests from any repository on GitHub. For more specific results, include the repository name in your prompt:\n\n  * `List all open issues assigned to me in OWNER/REPO`\n\n* Ask Copilot to work on an issue:\n\n  `I've been assigned this issue: https://github.com/octo-org/octo-repo/issues/1234. Start working on this for me in a suitably named branch.`\n\n* Ask Copilot to make file changes and raise a pull request on GitHub.com.\n\n  * `In the root of this repo, add a Node script called user-info.js that outputs information about the user who ran the script. Create a pull request to add this file to the repo on GitHub.`\n\n  * `Create a PR that updates the README at https://github.com/octo-org/octo-repo, changing the subheading \"How to run\" to \"Example usage\"`\n\n  Copilot creates a pull request on GitHub.com, on your behalf. You are marked as the pull request author.\n\n* Ask Copilot to create an issue for you on GitHub.com.\n\n  ``Raise an improvement issue in octo-org/octo-repo. In src/someapp/somefile.py the `file = open('data.txt', 'r')` block opens a file but never closes it.``\n\n* Ask Copilot to check the code changes in a pull request.\n\n  `Check the changes made in PR https://github.com/octo-org/octo-repo/pull/57575. Report any serious errors you find in these changes.`\n\n  Copilot responds in the CLI with a summary of any problems it finds.\n\n* Manage pull requests from GitHub Copilot CLI.\n\n  * `Merge all of the open PRs that I've created in octo-org/octo-repo`\n\n  * `Close PR #11 on octo-org/octo-repo`\n\n* Find specific types of issues.\n\n  `Use the GitHub MCP server to find good first issues for a new team member to work on from octo-org/octo-repo`\n\n  > [!NOTE]\n  > If you know that a specific MCP server can achieve a particular task, then specifying it in your prompt can help Copilot to deliver the results you want.\n\n* Find specific GitHub Actions workflows.\n\n  `List any Actions workflows in this repo that add comments to PRs`\n\n* Create a GitHub Actions workflow.\n\n  `Branch off from main and create a GitHub Actions workflow that will run on pull requests, or can be run manually. The workflow should run eslint to check for problems in the changes made in the PR. If warnings or errors are found these should be shown as messages in the diff view of the PR. I want to prevent code with errors from being merged into main so, if any errors are found, the workflow should cause the PR check to fail. Push the new branch and create a pull request.`\n\n## Steering the conversation\n\nYou can interact with Copilot while it's thinking to steer the conversation:\n\n* **Enqueue additional messages**: Send follow-up messages to steer the conversation in a different direction, or queue additional instructions for Copilot to process after it finishes its current response. This makes conversations feel more natural and keeps you in control.\n* **Inline feedback on rejection**: When you reject a tool permission request, you can give Copilot inline feedback about the rejection so it can adapt its approach without stopping entirely. This makes the conversation flow more naturally when you want to guide Copilot away from certain actions.\n\n## Automatic context management\n\nGitHub Copilot CLI automatically manages your conversation\n\n<note>Content truncated.     "content": "Contents of https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/set-up-copilot-cli/install-copilot-cli:\n# Installing GitHub Copilot CLI\n\nLearn how to install Copilot CLI so that you can use Copilot directly from the command line.\n\nTo find out about Copilot CLI before you install it, see [GitHub Copilot CLI](/en/copilot/concepts/copilot-surfaces/copilot-cli).\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n* **An active GitHub Copilot subscription**. See [Copilot plans](https://github.com/features/copilot/plans?ref_product=copilot\\&ref_type=engagement\\&ref_style=text).\n* (On Windows) **PowerShell** v6 or higher\n\nIf you have access to GitHub Copilot via your organization or enterprise, you cannot use Copilot CLI if your organization owner or enterprise administrator has disabled it in the organization or enterprise settings. See [Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization](/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-for-organization/manage-policies).\n\n## Installing or updating Copilot CLI\n\nYou can install Copilot CLI using WinGet (Windows), Homebrew (macOS and Linux), npm (all platforms), or an install script (macOS and Linux).\n\n### Installing with npm (all platforms)\n\nPrerequisite: Node.js 22 or later.\n\n```shell copy\nnpm install -g @github/copilot\n```\n\n> [!NOTE]\n> If you have `ignore-scripts=true` in your `~/.npmrc` file, you must use the command:\n>\n> ```shell copy\n> npm_config_ignore_scripts=false npm install -g @github/copilot\n> ```\n\nTo install the prerelease version:\n\n```shell copy\nnpm install -g @github/copilot@prerelease\n```\n\n### Installing with WinGet (Windows)\n\n```powershell copy\nwinget install GitHub.Copilot\n```\n\nTo install the prerelease version:\n\n```powershell copy\nwinget install GitHub.Copilot.Prerelease\n```\n\n### Installing with Homebrew (macOS and Linux)\n\n```shell copy\nbrew install --cask copilot-cli\n```\n\nTo install the prerelease version:\n\n```shell copy\nbrew install --cask copilot-cli@prerelease\n```\n\n### Installing with the install script (macOS and Linux)\n\n```shell copy\ncurl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash\n```\n\nOr:\n\n```shell copy\nwget -qO- https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash\n```\n\nTo run as root and install to `/usr/local/bin`, use `| sudo bash`.\n\nTo install to a custom directory, set the `PREFIX` environment variable. It defaults to `/usr/local` when run as root or `$HOME/.local` when run as a non-root user.\n\nTo install a specific version, set the `VERSION` environment variable. It defaults to the latest version.\n\nFor example, to install version `v0.0.369` to a custom directory:\n\n```shell copy\ncurl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | VERSION=\"v0.0.369\" PREFIX=\"$HOME/custom\" bash\n```\n\n### Download from GitHub.com\n\nYou can download the executables directly from [the `copilot-cli` repository](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/releases/).\n\nDownload the executable for your platform, unpack it, and run.\n\n## Authenticating with Copilot CLI\n\nOn first launch, if you're not currently logged in to GitHub, you'll be prompted to use the `/login` slash command. Enter this command and follow the on-screen instructions to authenticate. For more information on the authentication process, see [Authenticating GitHub Copilot CLI](/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/set-up-copilot-cli/authenticate-copilot-cli).\n\n### Authenticating with a personal access token\n\nYou can also authenticate using a fine-grained personal access token with the \"Copilot Requests\" permission enabled.\n\n1. Visit [Fine-grained personal access tokens](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new).\n2. Under **Resource owner**, select your **personal account**. Do not select an organization. The **Copilot Requests** permission is only available on user-owned fine-grained personal access tokens.\n3. Under **Repository access**, select the level of access appropriate for your use case:\n   * **Public repositories** if you only need to work with public repos.\n   * **All repositories** if you need access across all your current and future repos.\n   * **Only select repositories** if you want to restrict access to specific repos.\n4. Under **Permissions**, select the **Account** tab.\n5. Click **Add permissions** and select **Copilot Requests**.\n6. Click **Generate token**.\n7. Export the token in your terminal or environment configuration. Use the `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, or `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable (in order of precedence).\n\n## Next steps\n\nYou can now use Copilot from the command line. See [Using GitHub Copilot CLI](/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/overview).\n\nFor a list of commands for Copilot CLI, including the command to update, see [GitHub Copilot CLI command reference](/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-command-reference)."

Each token is priced based on the model used, and the total is converted into AI credits, where 1 AI credit = $0.01 USD.\n\nThe cost of an interaction depends on two things: the model and the number of tokens consumed.\n\nHow Copilot usage is tracked and billed depends on your plan type:\n\n* Individual plans (Copilot Free, Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, and Copilot Max) include GitHub AI Credits allowances that vary by plan. For details, see [Usage-based billing for individuals](/en/copilot/concepts/billing-and-usage/individuals/billing).\n* Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise include per-user GitHub AI Credits allowances that are pooled at the billing entity level. For details, see [Usage-based billing for organizations and enterprises](/en/copilot/concepts/billing-and-usage/organizations-and-enterprises/billing).\n\nWhen usage exceeds the included allowances for any Copilot plan, additional usage is billed in GitHub AI Credits at the per-token rates shown in the pricing tables below (1 AI credit = $0.01 USD).\n\nIf you purchased Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, or Copilot Max through an in-app purchase on iOS or Android, you can't buy additional GitHub AI Credits through the app store. However, if your GitHub account has a payment method on file, additional paid usage beyond your included AI credits is billed to that payment method based on your budget settings.\n\nTo avoid charges beyond your plan, create or edit a **Bundled AI credits budget**, set it to $0 USD, and enable **Stop usage when budget limit is reached**. Here is the raw content:\nContents of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/copilot-sdk/v1.0.29/docs/auth/server-to-server-tokens.md:\n# Server-to-server authentication\n\nUse a short-lived installation access token when a service needs to make Copilot requests on behalf of an organization without a user's credentials. In GitHub Actions, use the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` instead.\n\n## GitHub Actions\n\nFor workflows in an organization-owned repository, grant the built-in token permission to make Copilot requests:\n\n```yaml\npermissions:\n  contents: read\n  copilot-requests: write\n\njobs:\n  copilot:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - uses: actions/checkout@v6\n      - run: your-application\n        env:\n          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}\n```\n\nThe organization's **Allow use of Copilot CLI billed to the organization** policy must be enabled. This approach needs no GitHub App or stored authentication secret. For details, see [Using Copilot CLI in GitHub Actions with GITHUB_TOKEN](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli-in-actions).\n\n## Other services and CI systems\n\nFor services outside GitHub Actions:\n\n1. Create a GitHub App with the **Copilot Requests** organization permission set to **Read-only**.\n1. Install it on the organization that usage should be attributed and billed to.\n1. [Create an installation access token](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-an-installation-access-token-for-a-github-app) with the Copilot permission:\n\n   ```json\n   {\n     \"permissions\": {\n       \"organization_copilot_requests\": \"read\"\n     }\n   }\n   ```\n\n1. Pass the resulting `ghs_` token to the SDK's `gitHubToken`, `github_token`, or equivalent option. For an existing runtime URI, set it as `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` on the runtime process instead.\n\nThe organization must be enabled for Copilot requests from GitHub App installations. Installation tokens expire after one hour.\n\n> [!NOTE]\n> No signed-in user is required. `useLoggedInUser: false` turns off automatic credential discovery, including environment variable tokens such as `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, so pass the installation token through the SDK's explicit token option.\n\n## Configure the runtime\n\nThe following examples assume the minted token is in `INSTALLATION_TOKEN`. They pass it only to the child runtime and disable fallback to stored user credentials.\n\n<details open>\n<summary><strong>TypeScript</strong></summary>\n\n<!-- docs-validate: strict -->\n```typescript\nimport { CopilotClient, RuntimeConnection } from \"@github/copilot-sdk\";\n\nconst token = process.env.INSTALLATION_TOKEN;\nif (!token) throw new Error(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN is required\");\n\nconst client = new CopilotClient({\n    connection: RuntimeConnection.forStdio(),\n    gitHubToken: token,\n    useLoggedInUser: false,\n});\n```\n\n</details>\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Python</strong></summary>\n\n```python\nimport os\n\nfrom copilot import CopilotClient, RuntimeConnection\n\nclient = CopilotClient(\n    connection=RuntimeConnection.for_stdio(),\n    github_token=os.environ[\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN\"],\n    use_logged_in_user=False,\n)\n```\n\n</details>\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Go</strong></summary>\n\n```go\npackage main\n\nimport (\n\t\"log\"\n\t\"os\"\n\n\tcopilot \"github.com/github/copilot-sdk/go\"\n)\n\nfunc main() {\n\ttoken, ok := os.LookupEnv(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN\")\n\tif !ok {\n\t\tlog.Fatal(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN is required\")\n\t}\n\tclient := copilot.NewClient(&copilot.ClientOptions{\n\t\tConnection:      copilot.StdioConnection{},\n\t\tGitHubToken:     token,\n\t\tUseLoggedInUser: copilot.Bool(false),\n\t})\n\t_ = client\n}\n```\n\n</details>\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Rust</strong></summary>\n\n```rust\nuse github_copilot_sdk::{ClientOptions, Transport};\n\nfn main() {\n    let token = std::env::var(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN\").expect(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN is required\");\n    let options = ClientOptions::new()\n        .with_transport(Transport::Stdio)\n        .with_github_token(token)\n        .with_use_logged_in_user(false);\n    drop(options);\n}\n```\n\n</details>\n<details>\n<summary><strong>.NET</strong></summary>\n\n```csharp\nusing GitHub.Copilot;\n\nvar token = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN\")\n    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN is required\");\n\nawait using var client = new CopilotClient(new CopilotClientOptions\n{\n    Connection = RuntimeConnection.ForStdio(),\n    GitHubToken = token,\n    UseLoggedInUser = false,\n});\n```\n\n</details>\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Java</strong></summary>\n\n```java\nimport com.github.copilot.CopilotClient;\nimport com.github.copilot.rpc.CopilotClientOptions;\nimport java.util.Objects;\n\nvar token = Objects.requireNonNull(\n    System.getenv(\"INSTALLATION_TOKEN\"), \"INSTALLATION_TOKEN is required\");\n\ntry (var client = new CopilotClient(new CopilotClientOptions()\n        .setGitHubToken(token)\n        .setUseLoggedInUser(false))) {\n    // Use the client.\n}\n```\n\n</details>\n\nFor in-process FFI, use the same token option; environment variable tokens in the host process are ignored when `useLoggedInUser` is false. Only the most recent request survives.\n\nWatch for the outcome through the `session.model_change` event on success or the ephemeral `session.auto_tier_switch_failed` event on failure. A failed activation leaves the incumbent effective tier unchanged. Read the authoritative committed, pending, and activating preferences at any time through the session's `model.getCurrent` RPC method.\n\n```python\nfrom copilot import ModelSwitchAutoTierStatus\n\nresult = await session.set_auto_tier(\"intelligence\")\nif result.status == ModelSwitchAutoTierStatus.PENDING:\n    ...  # Accepted, but not yet in effect.\n\n# Return to the provider's default Auto routing.\nawait session.set_auto_tier(None)\n```\n\n`set_model()` accepts the same preference through its `auto_tier` argument, which stages the tier atomically with selecting `auto`. Pass `None` to return to provider-default routing, or omit the argument to leave the current preference unchanged.\n\nSee [Auto tier persistence](../docs/features/session-persistence.md#auto-tier-persistence) for the full lifecycle rules.\n\n## Image Support\n\nThe SDK supports image attachments via the `attachments` parameter. You can attach images by providing their file path, or by passing base64-encoded data directly using a blob attachment:\n\n<!-- docs-validate: hidden -->\n<!--\n```python\nimport base64\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nbase64_image_data = base64.b64encode(Path(\"/path/to/image.png\").read_bytes()).decode(\"ascii\")\n\n# File attachment — runtime reads from disk\nawait session.send(\n    \"What's in this image?\",\n    attachments=[\n        {\n            \"type\": \"file\",\n            \"path\": \"/path/to/image.jpg\",\n        }\n    ],\n)\n\n# Blob attachment — provide base64 data directly\nawait session.send(\n    \"What's in this image?\",\n    attachments=[\n        {\n            \"type\": \"blob\",\n            \"data\": base64_image_data,\n            \"mimeType\": \"image/png\",\n        }\n    ],\n)\n```\n-->\n<!-- /docs-validate: hidden -->\n\n```python\n# File attachment — runtime reads from disk\nawait session.send(\n    \"What's in this image?\",\n    attachments=[\n        {\n            \"type\": \"file\",\n            \"path\": \"/path/to/image.jpg\",\n        }\n    ],\n)\n\n# Blob attachment — provide base64 data directly\nawait session.send(\n    \"What's in this image?\",\n    attachments=[\n        {\n            \"type\": \"blob\",\n            \"data\": base64_image_data,\n            \"mimeType\": \"image/png\",\n        }\n    ],\n)\n```\n\nSupported image formats are PNG, JPEG, WebP, and GIF. Images in other formats, such as BMP or TIFF, are not sent to the model. The agent's `view` tool can also read images directly from the filesystem, so you can also ask questions like:\n\n```python\nawait session.send(\"What does the most recent jpg in this directory portray?\")\n```\n\n## Structured output (experimental)\n\nUse a Pydantic model, just like custom-tool parameter schemas:\n\n```python\nfrom pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict\n\n\nclass Inventory(BaseModel):\n    model_config = ConfigDict(extra=\"forbid\")\n    count: int\n    color: str\n\n\ninventory = await session.send_and_wait_typed(\n    \"Call get_inventory, then report the widget count and color.\",\n    Inventory,\n)\nprint(inventory.count, inventory.color)\n```\n\nThe helper derives a JSON Schema using `model_json_schema()` and validates the\nfinal JSON with `model_validate_json(by_alias=True, by_name=False)` so validation\nuses the schema's alias names, including in nested models, regardless of\nmodel-level alias settings. This requires Pydantic 2.11 or newer.\nFor explicit schemas, use\n`send(prompt, response_schema=schema)` or `send_and_wait(prompt,\nresponse_schema=schema)`; the latter returns the ordinary message event.\n`response_schema` also accepts a Pydantic model class without parsing the result.\n\nThe schema applies to one run, including tools, steering, and stop-hook\ncorrections, not subsequent independent sends or subagents. Streaming remains\ntext. Structured waits select the last root message without tool requests whose\n`originating_message_id` matches the admitted message, at non-autopilot idle\nor the matching root `session.autopilot_stopped` event.\nAll `send_and_wait` variants accept this authoritative Autopilot terminal without\nwaiting for or stopping attached shells. Its `request_id` must match the original\nsend ID; continuation messages do not change ownership. Missing, unrelated, or\nsubagent terminals cannot complete the wait. `session.idle` remains whole-session\nquiescence; `assistant.idle` and `session.task_complete` alone are not completion.\nConcurrent structured waits keep their own results; later queued work can delay\nidle. Aborts, session errors after the run starts, or missing final output fail\nthe wait. Timeout/cancellation only stops waiting, not agent work. Immediate\nsteering cannot specify a schema.\n\nProvider schema restrictions still apply: use closed objects (as above) and\nrequired fields for strict OpenAI output. Schemas are not rewritten; unsupported\nmodels/schemas produce errors. Low-level `session.rpc.send` and\n`session.rpc.send_messages` expose the full `ResponseFormat` options.\n\n## Streaming\n\nEnable streaming to receive assistant response chunks as they're generated:\n\n```python\nimport asyncio\n\nfrom copilot import CopilotClient\nfrom copilot.session_events import (\n    AssistantMessageData,\n    AssistantMessageDeltaData,\n    AssistantReasoningData,\n    AssistantReasoningDeltaData,\n    SessionAutopilotStoppedData,\n    SessionIdleData,\n    SessionMode,\n)\nfrom copilot.session import PermissionHandler\n\n\nasync def main():\n    async with CopilotClient() as client:\n        async with await client.create_session(\n            on_permission_request=PermissionHandler.approve_all,\n            model=\"gpt-5\",\n            streaming=True,\n        ) as session:\n            # Wait for non-Autopilot idle or this request's Autopilot stop\n            request_id = None\n            pending = []\n            done = asyncio.Event()\n\n            def observe(event):\n                match event.data:\n                    case AssistantMessageDeltaData() as data:\n                        # Streaming message chunk - print incrementally\n                        delta = data.delta_content or \"\"\n                        print(delta, end=\"\", flush=True)\n                    case AssistantReasoningDeltaData() as data:\n    \n\n<note>Content truncated. Call the fetch tool with a start_index of 48500 to get more content.</note>"

## 2026-11-07T15:06:47.938Z - assistant.message

Event ID: `0f876f56-1060-49a1-830d-4d16bfb2d73c`

**Yes—the official GitHub Copilot Python SDK can fit behind the existing provider interface without rewriting the six agents or orchestration. It is not a completely equivalent drop-in:** budget enforcement, model settings and usage accounting need particular care.

I checked the published **`github-copilot-sdk` 1.0.29** and its official source. The SDK is not installed here; a Copilot CLI shim exists, but its authentication and compatibility are unverified. Nothing was installed, switched or executed against a model.

### Compatibility assessment

| Area | Findings |
|---|---|
| **Authentication** | Supports stored Copilot CLI OAuth credentials, explicit GitHub user tokens and environment-token discovery. Fine-grained PATs require the **Copilot Requests** account permission; classic PATs are unsupported. Desktop Copilot access alone does not establish that the SDK can authenticate. [Authentication](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/v1.0.29/docs/auth/authenticate.md) |
| **Subscription and policy** | Standard user authentication requires Copilot entitlement and available usage allowance. Organization/enterprise policy must permit CLI use and the selected model. BYOK avoids Copilot entitlement but still requires a provider key, so it does not solve the missing OpenAI-key problem. Organization-attributed service authentication exists but would unnecessarily expand this assignment. [Prerequisites](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/set-up-copilot-cli/install-copilot-cli) |
| **Structured responses** | The release supports **provider-native JSON Schema**, through `send_and_wait(..., response_schema=...)`, plus a Pydantic typed helper. This feature is explicitly experimental; unsupported models/schemas fail. We can reuse the existing closed-object schema conversion and coordinator validation rather than parse prose. [Python SDK](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/v1.0.29/python/README.md#structured-output-experimental) |
| **Token reporting** | `assistant.usage` events expose per-model-call input/output usage, including calls within a runtime turn sequence. Subscribe before sending and preserve every event. Cache counts are already included in input tokens; missing counts must remain unknown, not become zero. Events are ephemeral, making immediate persistence important. [Usage reporting](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/v1.0.29/docs/features/usage-and-billing.md) |
| **Tool and context restrictions** | Supported, but **default SDK configuration is inappropriate**: it exposes coding-runtime capabilities. Use `mode="empty"`, isolated runtime storage, an explicit empty tool allowlist and deny-by-default permissions. Disable discovery, skills, memory, cross-session retrieval and plugins. Empty mode supplies restrictive defaults. [Isolation configuration](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/v1.0.29/python/copilot/_mode.py) |
| **Budgets and cancellation** | One SDK send can trigger multiple model calls. Cancelling the wait does **not** stop runtime work; the adapter must explicitly abort it. SDK AI-credit limits are post-call soft caps, not strict request/token ceilings. [Agent loop](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/v1.0.29/docs/features/agent-loop.md), [Session limits](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/v1.0.29/docs/features/session-limits.md) |

### Minimum changes

1. **Provider adapter in `llm.py`.** Implement the existing `StructuredLLM` interface using one shared Copilot client and a fresh, isolated session per operation. Supply the existing system prompt and response schema; collect usage before returning raw JSON for coordinator validation. Explicitly abort timed-out work and preserve failures.

2. **Keep simulated tools outside the SDK.** Set `available_tools=[]`. The existing coordinator continues executing logs, metrics, changes, dependencies and history; the model only proposes structured queries. Registering those tools directly with Copilot would introduce a second investigation loop and undermine the existing enforcement.

3. **Small setup/evaluator wiring changes.** Replace the provider dependency with a pinned SDK/runtime version, update construction and cleanup in `cli.py`/`evaluate.py`, and record the actual provider, model, runtime and settings in the manifest. No agent-prompt or orchestration redesign is needed.

4. **Focused adapter regressions.** Cover schema failure, usage preservation, concurrent-session isolation, denied tools/context discovery, cancellation and actual backend-call accounting.

### Evaluation limitations that must remain explicit

- **Exact budget parity is the main unresolved issue.** The coordinator currently counts adapter calls. Copilot can make additional model turns or runtime retries. We must verify a single-call configuration or add narrowly scoped accounting/enforcement; counting SDK sends as provider requests would be misleading.
- I found no public temperature parameter equivalent to the current OpenAI setting in the reviewed create/send APIs. Output-limit overrides exist, but their enforcement also needs verification. We must not claim temperature 0 or identical output ceilings merely by putting those values in metadata.
- Both approaches can still be compared fairly using the **same Copilot model, runtime and effective settings**, but those results would be a new provider configuration—not interchangeable with an OpenAI benchmark.
- Empty mode and tool restrictions provide application-level isolation, **not an OS sandbox**. Evaluator files must stay outside the runtime working directory and all model-facing inputs.
- Copilot usage consumes allowance/AI credits and may incur charges. The earlier OpenAI approval and dollar estimate do **not** authorize a Copilot batch.

**Recommendation:** feasible, provided those accounting and isolation checks pass; otherwise the strict budget requirement must be disclosed as incomplete. The original OpenAI batch remains paused. Separately, clean installation and the documented offline CLI commands succeeded with **195 tests passing**; the temporary environment was removed.

    "description": "Reconcile actual cached token usage, calculate pilot costs and inspect private scoring criteria"
  },

Temperature is explicitly 0 by default; use\r\n`--temperature` to change it for either approach or the evaluator.\r\nThere is no browser, frontend, database, vector\r\nsearch, Docker, external investigation API, or agent framework. The only remote\r\nAPI is the explicitly requested LLM provider. `store=False` is used. The model\r\nreceives observations through prompts and cannot execute tools or read files.\r\n\r\n## Small module map\r\n\r\n| File | Responsibility |\r\n| --- | --- |\r\n| `models.py` | Typed tool, task, agent, plan, Critic objection, report, budget and trace contracts |\r\n| `tools.py` | Five async, read-only simulated tools with provenance, coverage and failure injection |\r\n| `agents.py` | Readable six-role prompts, response schemas, access map and suggested query windows |\r\n| `investigation.py` | Shared state, serialized coordinator, bounded workers and multi-agent loop |\r\n| `baseline.py` | One iterative agent using the same coordinator, tools and report schema |\r\n| `llm.py` | OpenAI strict JSON-schema adapter and explicitly scripted test double |\r\n| `cli.py` | Collection/investigation commands and persisted report/trace output |\r\n| `evaluate.py` | Paired/repeated evaluation, deterministic limited scoring, JSON/CSV and summary |\r\n| `data/incidents.json` | Ten agent-visible incidents, neutral IDs and symptom-only alerts |\r\n| `data/simulation.json` | Runtime-only failure/latency settings, never passed to agents |\r\n| `data/evaluation/ground_truth.json` | Evaluator-only answers/tags, never loaded by investigation code |\r\n| `data/evaluation/rubric.json` | Private fact patterns, categories and evidence relationships |\r\n| `tests/` | Foundation checks, mocked collaboration, retries, safeguards and CLI persistence |\r\n\r\n## Architecture and collaboration\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nflowchart TD\r\n    CLI[CLI: multi-agent or baseline] --> C[Serialized coordinator: dependencies / budgets / retries]\r\n    C --> O[Orchestrator: structured initial plan]\r\n    O --> P{Independent evidence tasks run concurrently}\r\n    P --> A[Observability: logs and metrics]\r\n    P --> D[Dependency: changes / dependencies / history]\r\n    T[Five local tools: incidents.json] --> P\r\n    A --> S[Shared evidence ledger and structured findings]\r\n    D --> S\r\n    S --> R[Reasoning: compare hypotheses]\r\n    R --> K[Critic: objections and discriminating queries]\r\n    K --> Q[Orchestrator: continue or finish]\r\n    Q -->|selected valid follow-ups, at most two rounds| P\r\n    Q -->|finish or limit| F[Reporting: grounded or inconclusive]\r\n    F --> OUT[Saved report and execution trace]\r\n    C --> B[Baseline: one iterative agent]\r\n    B -->|choose tools / inspect / revise| T\r\n    B --> OUT\r\n    L[Shared OpenAI client and model] -. structured responses .-> O\r\n    L -.-> A\r\n    L -.-> D\r\n    L -.-> R\r\n    L -.-> K\r\n    L -.-> Q\r\n    L -.-> F\r\n    L -.-> B\r\n    G[Evaluator-only ground truth and rubric] --> E[Evaluation: deterministic limited scores]\r\n    OUT --> E\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe Orchestrator proposes independent `initial-` evidence tasks covering all five\r\nfamilies. Runtime validation prevents cross-incident queries, forbidden role/tool\r\ncombinations, duplicate queries, invalid IDs/dependencies and model-selected retry\r\nlimits. Tool workers return values; only the coordinator applies results to state.\r\nThe two specialist summaries also run concurrently on frozen snapshots.\r\n\r\nReasoning proposes ranked alternatives with citations and assumptions. Critic\r\nnames unsupported hypotheses and requests specific queries. Orchestrator chooses\r\nrequest indices or stops. Valid follow-ups receive explicit dependencies on the\r\ndecision and relevant successful analysis. Reasoning then revises using the new\r\nobservations and objections. If no worthwhile query is requested, no follow-up is\r\nperformed. The mocked demo widens a previously narrow configuration query in\r\nresponse to a Critic objection, then revises the hypothesis.\r\n\r\nBoth approaches validate revision history. A retained hypothesis ID must keep every\r\npreviously cited evidence ID, including counterevidence. Reclassification between\r\nsupporting and contradicting evidence, or rejection of a hypothesis, requires an\r\nexplicit explanation. This checks preservation, not whether the explanation is\r\nconvincing. An invalid or failed revision cannot overwrite the last successful\r\nhypotheses; an inconclusive runtime fallback preserves those validated candidates.\r\n\r\nQuery deduplication canonicalizes service order and UTC timestamps. Identical\r\ncompleted queries are rejected; a changed window/filter/limit is a distinct query,\r\nallowing targeted investigation. Deliberate identical retries require an eligible\r\nprior error, an explicit retry flag and remaining per-query attempts. Changing\r\nscope can still produce overlapping records: evidence IDs deduplicate records\r\nwithout erasing per-query provenance.\r\n\r\nReporting has no tool access. Runtime requires reported hypotheses to be exact\r\ncopies of the latest Reasoning hypotheses (a ranked subset is allowed, but must\r\nretain the top-ranked candidate as the winner of a ranked report); it cannot\r\ninvent citations, claims, confidence or assumptions. Ranked hypotheses require\r\nsupporting observations. Citation existence is checked, **not semantic entailment**:\r\nthe Critic provides model-based scrutiny, not a proof. Unresolved critical objections,\r\nmissing critical analysis, terminal source failures or inability to produce a valid\r\nreport force an inconclusive outcome with explicit limitations. A missing model\r\nreport yields a clearly marked runtime fallback, not a diagnosis.\r\n\r\nThe baseline repeatedly chooses queries, inspects results, revises hypotheses and\r\nfinishes using the same report schema. Its tool calls execute sequentially. It gets\r\nthe same incident context, suggested windows, tool records and total resource\r\nceilings, without separate specialist/Critic roles. Each CLI run creates fresh tools,\r\nresetting injected failures. Evaluation must use the same model, settings and budget\r\nand a fresh tool instance for each approach.\r\n\r\n## Runtime ceilings and recovery\r\n\r\n| Ceiling | Default (both approaches) |\r\n| --- | --- |\r\n| Total tool calls | 30 |\r\n| Total LLM calls, including transient failures | 24 |\r\n| Total charged/reserved tokens | 120,000 |\r\n| Maximum output tokens per model call | 1,500 |\r\n| Overall investigation deadline | 120 seconds |\r\n| Per tool / per model timeout | 2 / 30 seconds |\r\n| Concurrent tools | 5 (baseline deliberately sequential) |\r\n| Attempts per transiently failing operation/query | 3 total, not 3 retries |\r\n| Critic-driven follow-up rounds | 2 maximum |\r\n\r\n`ExecutionBudget` is injectable through either Python runner; the CLI uses these\r\ndefaults. The baseline's iterative steps are bounded by the same LLM-call ceiling.\r\nThe original low-level `TaskSpec` accepts up to five attempts for compatibility\r\nwith foundation tests; agent/baseline runs always override it with the runtime\r\nthree-attempt ceiling, shared across identical queries.\r\n\r\nSDK retries are disabled. Connection/timeout, HTTP 408/429 and server failures are\r\nretryable while resources remain. Authentication, refusal, incomplete output,\r\ninvalid schemas/references/access and exhausted budgets are not retryable. Model\r\nretry waits are bounded; local fixture tools need no backoff. Failed prerequisites\r\nblock dependents. Independent sources can continue, and analyses can inspect error\r\nobservations through successful-task dependencies rather than pretend a failed\r\ntool succeeded. Terminal failures are reported conservatively as inconclusive.\r\nTool batches execute prerequisite-ready waves, regardless of input order, including\r\nin sequential mode. Blocked tasks have a structured dependency error and zero\r\nattempts. Adapter integration errors are visible, nonretryable operation failures,\r\nnot empty successes. Model-call, attempt and token reservations share one atomic\r\nbudget check. Responses are checked against the deadline before admission, and\r\nfinalization cannot return ordinary success after the overall deadline.\r\n\r\nBefore dispatch, the coordinator reserves a conservative UTF-8 byte-based bound\r\nfor input text and schema plus overhead and maximum output tokens. This is\r\ndeliberately more conservative than typical tokenizer counts. Returned provider\r\nusage replaces reservations, even when response validation fails. Calls with\r\nunknown provider usage retain their full reservation, listed separately from\r\nmeasured input/output tokens. A provider discrepancy exceeding the reservation\r\nterminates that operation explicitly rather than silently ignoring usage. The\r\nreservation is a preflight estimate, not a guaranteed provider-side spending cap:\r\nhidden provider overhead and already accepted work cannot be undone.\r\nMock scripts consume zero real LLM tokens; their counters are **not** performance\r\nmeasurements of a real model. Timeout cannot undo work already accepted by the\r\nprovider, so unknown usage is charged conservatively.\r\nCancellation of a public investigation runner returns an inconclusive run with\r\na cancellation trace, allowing the CLI to persist interrupted investigations.\r\nCompleted sibling tool results and returned provider usage survive cancellation\r\nof a parallel batch; genuinely unknown usage alone retains the full reservation.\r\n\r\n## Tool semantics and evaluator separation\r\n\r\nAll source/query windows are timezone-aware and half-open `[start, end)`.\r\nFilters select emitting/calling services; an empty service filter means all\r\nservices covered by that source, not all services in the system. Request a service\r\nexplicitly to expose missing service coverage. Historical incidents use their own\r\npast timestamps; suggested history queries use a 90-day lookback.\r\n\r\nEvery tool result preserves source, original query, collection time, observed\r\nintervals/gaps, covered/missing services, matched/returned counts and truncation.\r\nA covered empty query is `complete`; unavailable scope or truncation is `partial`\r\nwith issues; a failure is `error` with code/message/retryability and no claimed\r\nobservations. Source coverage denotes retention, not omniscience or continuous\r\nmeasurement. Unknown dependency health is not a healthy dependency.\r\n\r\nInjected failures follow `normalized-query-first-n-attempts-v1`: the first N\r\nattempts of **each distinct normalized query** fail when its incident/tool family\r\nhas a configured rule. `failures: null` always fails. Service order and UTC-equivalent\r\ntimestamps share query identity. Different windows, filters or limits have separate\r\nattempt counters; querying another family or query cannot consume their failures.\r\nEvery approach/repetition gets a fresh tool instance with identical settings.\r\nThis replaces the older incident/family-global attempt counter. There is no random\r\nfault seed to tune; outcomes for a given query/attempt are deterministic.\r\n\r\nThe ten incidents include misleading changes/history, conflicting scopes, incomplete\r\ndata, transient failure and an intentionally inconclusive case. Ground-truth labels\r\nare evaluator-only. This is input separation, not OS-level isolation: model clients\r\nnever receive evaluator files or arbitrary filesystem access. There is no\r\ncase-specific answer logic. Files under `tests/fixtures/` contain explicit scripted\r\nexample outputs solely for testing; never use them as prediction/evaluation results.\r\n\r\n## Evaluation commands and reproducibility\r\n\r\nDefault evaluation uses all ten incidents and both approaches. Configure repeats,\r\nthe shared model/temperature, and optionally a local JSON `ExecutionBudget`. Each\r\nincident run gets the same total ceilings; these are not a total batch spending\r\nlimit. A batch contains two times incident count times repeats runs, each with up\r\nto 24 model calls by default. **Do not run paid evaluation without approving that\r\nspend. The completed pilot does not authorize a full batch or repeats.**\r\n\r\n```powershell\r\n# Offline plumbing tests only; no provider requests:\r\n.\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe -m pytest tests\\test_evaluate.py\r\n\r\n# PAID pilot: only after explicit approval; always choose a fresh output directory:\r\n.\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe evaluate.py --mode live --allow-paid --model gpt-4.1-mini --temperature 0 --incidents inc-001 --repeats 1 --output-dir outputs\\pilot-new\r\n\r\n# PAID full batch: separate approval is required; one run per approach per incident:\r\n.\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe evaluate.py --mode live --allow-paid --repeats 1 --output-dir outputs\\evaluation-live\r\n\r\n# Optional configuration:\r\n.\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe evaluate.py --mode live --allow-paid --model gpt-4.1-mini --temperature 0 --repeats 2 --budget budget.json --output-dir outputs\\evaluation-custom\r\n```\r\n\r\n`--incidents inc-001 inc-009` selects a subset for a smoke test; selection is recorded\r\nand absent case types have null rates. `--mode mocked --mock-script-dir PATH`\r\nrequires one explicit script named `inc-001.multi-agent.json` / `inc-001.baseline.json`\r\n(and likewise for every selected incident). Missing scripts fail preflight; none\r\nare silently invented. Mocked batches identify `scripted-test-double`, store null\r\nprovider token measurements, and label summaries **plumbing only, not LLM performance**.\r\nThere is no LLM judge and no fabricated all-incident prediction script.\r\n\r\nUse a **new output directory** for every batch. Outputs are:\r\n`manifest.json`, `results.json`, `results.csv`, `summary.md`, and individual\r\n`runs\\INCIDENT.APPROACH.REPETITION\\report.json` / `trace.json`.\r\n`runs.jsonl` journals completed rows, including failures, so interrupted batches\r\nretain completed work. A partial batch has no completed comparison summary;\r\nautomatic resume/merging is intentionally not implemented.\r\n\r\nThe manifest captures the full planned order, selected incidents, repeats, shared\r\nmodel settings/budget, Python/dependency versions, implementation/data/rubric hashes\r\nand failure-policy version. Pair order alternates across incidents/repetitions to\r\nreduce systematic warm-up/order bias; runs are not executed as competing parallel\r\nbenchmarks. Provider caching/availability and model aliases can still vary.\r\nUse a provider-pinned model identifier where available. Temperature 0 does not\r\nguarantee identical provider responses or latency.\r\n\r\n## Deterministic, limited scoring rubric\r\n\r\n`data/evaluation/rubric.json` contains expected facts, bounded case-specific English\r\npatterns (all required patterns must match; listed rejection patterns veto a match),\r\nand curated positive/negative evidence relationships. All of it is evaluator-only.\r\nAgents see only the **same generic category vocabulary for every incident**:\r\n`connection_capacity`, `response_contract`, `upstream_availability`, `memory_capacity`,\r\n`name_resolution`, `queue_delivery`, `logging_backpressure`, `tls_validation`,\r\n`request_capacity`, and `unknown`. Categories alone never earn root-cause credit.\r\n\r\n| Metric | Definition and limits |\r\n| --- | --- |\r\n| Top-ranked root-cause accuracy | On answerable cases, a ranked top hypothesis must select the expected generic category and express all required distinguishing facts in its claim. Abstentions and terminal failures count as incorrect; every planned answerable row remains in the denominator. This is **rubric accuracy**, not arbitrary-prose semantic verification. |\r\n| Abstention frequency | Explicit inconclusive reports divided by all runs. Missing reports from crashes are listed separately, not credited as intentional decisions. |\r\n| Intentionally inconclusive handling | The inconclusive case must produce an inconclusive report with a recognized insufficiency explanation and no terminal execution/analysis failure. A provider-error fallback is abstention, but not correct analytical handling. |\r\n| Citation existence | Fraction of cited IDs present in that incident's source corpus, counted once per hypothesis/polarity. |\r\n| Citation availability | Fraction actually acquired into that run's ledger with matching source record content. Existing but uncollected IDs receive no availability credit. |\r\n| Support-link precision | A support citation must be available and explicitly linked to a recognized fact in that hypothesis's claim. A normal-database metric or similar historical incident cannot support the current configuration/DNS diagnosis merely because its ID exists. |\r\n| Counterevidence-link precision | Available contradicting citations must be listed as opposing a matched fact. Citing opposition as support earns no support credit. |\r\n| Rubric fact support | Fraction of recognized facts with a complete allowed support witness set. Some facts require joint witnesses, e.g. queue timeout configuration plus job duration. Counterevidence does not establish the positive claim. |\r\n| Tool calls | Runtime reservations/attempts, including retries/timeouts; checked against per-task attempt totals. No-dispatch budget errors add no tool call. |\r\n| Latency | Measured from per-run preparation and runner entry through completion/failure, including all analyses, retries and waiting; excludes batch setup and output-file I/O. From the project directory in PowerShell:\n \n ```powershell\n python -m venv .venv\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe -m pip install -e \".[dev]\"\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe -m pytest\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe cli.py list\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe cli.py collect inc-007\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe cli.py collect inc-006 --json\n \n # Explicitly MOCKED demo: these supplied replies are not real model reasoning.\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe cli.py run multi-agent inc-001 --mock-script tests\\fixtures\\multi_agent.json --output-dir outputs\\mock-multi\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe cli.py run baseline inc-001 --mock-script tests\\fixtures\\baseline.json --output-dir outputs\\mock-baseline\n ```\n \n On macOS/Linux use `.venv/bin/python` and the corresponding path separators.\n Editable installation expects the source checkout and adjacent JSON fixtures.\n Packaging a standalone wheel with bundled data is out of scope.\n \n Each `run` writes `report.json` and `trace.json`. Use a fresh output directory:\n existing outputs are never overwritten. Exit status is 0 for a ranked report,\n 2 for an inconclusive investigation, and nonzero for command/setup errors.\n The trace contains execution mode, model, ceilings, task IDs/dependencies/statuses,\n structured task outputs, every returned tool attempt, evidence, model prompts/raw\n structured responses, usage and failures. Treat traces as potentially sensitive\n when replacing synthetic data. Do not publish environment files or credentials.\n \n ## Live OpenAI runs (paid, explicit opt-in)\n \n OpenAI was selected for this stage. All six roles share one `AsyncOpenAI` client\n and model (`gpt-4.1-mini` by default); the baseline uses the same adapter and default\n model. Timeout cannot undo work already accepted by the\n provider, so unknown usage is charged conservatively.\n Cancellation of a public investigation runner returns an inconclusive run with\n a cancellation trace, allowing the CLI to persist interrupted investigations.\n Completed sibling tool results and returned provider usage survive cancellation\n of a parallel batch; genuinely unknown usage alone retains the full reservation.\n \n ## Tool semantics and evaluator separation\n \n All source/query windows are timezone-aware and half-open `[start, end)`.\n Filters select emitting/calling services; an empty service filter means all\n services covered by that source, not all services in the system. Request a service\n explicitly to expose missing service coverage. Historical incidents use their own\n past timestamps; suggested history queries use a 90-day lookback.\n \n Every tool result preserves source, original query, collection time, observed\n intervals/gaps, covered/missing services, matched/returned counts and truncation.\n A covered empty query is `complete`; unavailable scope or truncation is `partial`\n with issues; a failure is `error` with code/message/retryability and no claimed\n observations. Source coverage denotes retention, not omniscience or continuous\n measurement. Unknown dependency health is not a healthy dependency.\n \n Injected failures follow `normalized-query-first-n-attempts-v1`: the first N\n attempts of **each distinct normalized query** fail when its incident/tool family\n has a configured rule. `failures: null` always fails. Service order and UTC-equivalent\n timestamps share query identity. Different windows, filters or limits have separate\n attempt counters; querying another family or query cannot consume their failures.\n Every approach/repetition gets a fresh tool instance with identical settings.\n This replaces the older incident/family-global attempt counter. There is no random\n fault seed to tune; outcomes for a given query/attempt are deterministic.\n \n The ten incidents include misleading changes/history, conflicting scopes, incomplete\n data, transient failure and an intentionally inconclusive case. Ground-truth labels\n are evaluator-only. This is input separation, not OS-level isolation: model clients\n never receive evaluator files or arbitrary filesystem access. There is no\n case-specific answer logic. Files under `tests/fixtures/` contain explicit scripted\n example outputs solely for testing; never use them as prediction/evaluation results.\n \n ## Evaluation commands and reproducibility\n \n Default evaluation uses all ten incidents and both approaches. Configure repeats,\n the shared model/temperature, and optionally a local JSON `ExecutionBudget`. Each\n incident run gets the same total ceilings; these are not a total batch spending\n limit. A batch contains two times incident count times repeats runs, each with up\n to 24 model calls by default. **Do not run paid evaluation without approving that\n spend. The completed pilot does not authorize a full batch or repeats.**\n \n ```powershell\n # Offline plumbing tests only; no provider requests:\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe -m pytest tests\\test_evaluate.py\n \n # PAID pilot: only after explicit approval; always choose a fresh output directory:\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe evaluate.py --mode live --allow-paid --model gpt-4.1-mini --temperature 0 --incidents inc-001 --repeats 1 --output-dir outputs\\pilot-new\n \n # PAID full batch: separate approval is required; one run per approach per incident:\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe evaluate.py --mode live --allow-paid --repeats 1 --output-dir outputs\\evaluation-live\n \n # Optional configuration:\n .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe evaluate.py --mode live --allow-paid --model gpt-4.1-mini --temperature 0 --repeats 2 --budget budget.json --output-dir outputs\\evaluation-custom\n ```\n \n `--incidents inc-001 inc-009` selects a subset for a smoke test; selection is recorded\n and absent case types have null rates. `--mode mocked --mock-script-dir PATH`\n requires one explicit script named `inc-001.multi-agent.json` / `inc-001.baseline.json`\n (and likewise for every selected incident). Missing scripts fail preflight; none\n are silently invented. Mocked batches identify `scripted-test-double`, store null\n provider token measurements, and label summaries **plumbing only, not LLM performance**.\n There is no LLM judge and no fabricated all-incident prediction script.\n \n Use a **new output directory** for every batch. Outputs are:\n `manifest.json`, `results.json`, `results.csv`, `summary.md`, and individual\n `runs\\INCIDENT.APPROACH.REPETITION\\report.json` / `trace.json`.\n `runs.jsonl` journals completed rows, including failures, so interrupted batches\n retain completed work. A partial batch has no completed comparison summary;\n automatic resume/merging is intentionally not implemented.\n \n The manifest captures the full planned order, selected incidents, repeats, shared\n model settings/budget, Python/dependency versions, implementation/data/rubric hashes\n and failure-policy version. Pair order alternates across incidents/repetitions to\n reduce systematic warm-up/order bias; runs are not executed as competing parallel\n benchmarks. Provider caching/availability and model aliases can still vary.\n Use a provider-pinned model identifier where available. Temperature 0 does not\n guarantee identical provider responses or latency.\n \n ## Deterministic, limited scoring rubric\n \n `data/evaluation/rubric.json` contains expected facts, bounded case-specific English\n patterns (all required patterns must match; listed rejection patterns veto a match),\n and curated positive/negative evidence relationships. All of it is evaluator-only.\n Agents see only the **same generic category vocabulary for every incident**:\n `connection_capacity`, `response_contract`, `upstream_availability`, `memory_capacity`,\n `name_resolution`, `queue_delivery`, `logging_backpressure`, `tls_validation`,\n `request_capacity`, and `unknown`. Categories alone never earn root-cause credit.\n \n | Metric | Definition and limits |\n | --- | --- |\n | Top-ranked root-cause accuracy | On answerable cases, a ranked top hypothesis must select the expected generic category and express all required distinguishing facts in its claim. Abstentions and terminal failures count as incorrect; every planned answerable row remains in the denominator. This is **rubric accuracy**, not arbitrary-prose semantic verification. |\n | Abstention frequency | Explicit inconclusive reports divided by all runs. Missing reports from crashes are listed separately, not credited as intentional decisions. |\n | Intentionally inconclusive handling | The inconclusive case must produce an inconclusive report with a recognized insufficiency explanation and no terminal execution/analysis failure. A provider-error fallback is abstention, but not correct analytical handling. |\n | Citation existence | Fraction of cited IDs present in that incident's source corpus, counted once per hypothesis/polarity. |\n | Citation availability | Fraction actually acquired into that run's ledger with matching source record content. Existing but uncollected IDs receive no availability credit. |\n | Support-link precision | A support citation must be available and explicitly linked to a recognized fact in that hypothesis's claim. A normal-database metric or similar historical incident cannot support the current configuration/DNS diagnosis merely because its ID exists. |\n | Counterevidence-link precision | Available contradicting citations must be listed as opposing a matched fact. Citing opposition as support earns no support credit. |\n | Rubric fact support | Fraction of recognized facts with a complete allowed support witness set. Some facts require joint witnesses, e.g. queue timeout configuration plus job duration. Counterevidence does not establish the positive claim. |\n | Tool calls | Runtime reservations/attempts, including retries/timeouts; checked against per-task attempt totals. No-dispatch budget errors add no tool call. |\n | Latency | Measured from per-run preparation and runner entry through completion/failure, including all analyses, retries and waiting; excludes batch setup and output-file I/O. The oute\n"
  },
  "turnId": "4"
}
